title: Calculus II: Integration, Series & Applications
description: Advanced integration, applications of accumulation, sequences and series, and power-series approximations for quantitative science.

lessons.worked_example: If a spring-like actuator applies F(x)=4x N from x=0 to 3 m, W=∫₀³4x dx=18 J.

lessons.title: Power series and Taylor error
lessons.worked_example: For eˣ near x=0, the quadratic approximation at x=0.2 is 1+0.2+0.2²/2=1.22; the cubic remainder is under about 0.0017 on that interval.

lessons.title: Integrals as accumulation: total consumption from rate data, numerical rules with error bounds and improper integrals
lessons.worked_example: The exact total of 0.5e^(0.03t) over 0 to 48 h is 53.68 mmol; 12 h samples give a trapezoidal 54.26 (bound 1.09) and Simpson 53.68 mmol; a release rate 2.0e^(−0.1t) totals 20 μg over all time.

lessons.title: Taylor approximations with an error bound: when "approximately" is good enough
lessons.worked_example: At x = 0.2, P₂ for e^(−x) is 0.8200 against 0.8187, within the remainder bound 0.001333; linear decay overstates loss by 2.5% at kt = 0.05; 1 − kt stays within 0.01 of e^(−kt) for kt ≤ 0.141.

lessons.title: Integration methods and domain checks
lessons.worked_example: Compare the three structures 2t/(1+t²), xeˣ and 1/((x+1)(x+2)). The first matches a derivative divided by its original function and gives ln 5 on [0,2]. The second combines a polynomial and exponential; parts gives 1 on [0,1]. The third separates into reciprocal linear terms and gives ln(4/3) on [0,1]. Different numerical results are expected because these are three different integrands. For each, differentiate the proposed primitive, verify every denominator on the interval and only then evaluate the endpoints. A calculator value alone would not reveal a missing chain factor or an interval crossing a pole.

lessons.title: Improper integrals, singularities and comparison
lessons.worked_example: For q(t)=6/(1+t)², integrate first on [0,b]. The antiderivative is −6/(1+t), so the finite total is 6−6/(1+b). Taking b to infinity gives 6. If observations stop at t=3, the observed-window integral is 4.5 and the model-based remaining tail is 1.5. Their sum matches the total. Contrast this with q(t)=6/(1+t), whose finite-window integral is 6 ln(1+b). Its rate also tends to zero, but its unlimited total diverges. The difference comes from the tail exponent, not from whether the curve appears nearly flat on a finite plot.

lessons.title: Positive series and convergence tests
lessons.worked_example: Suppose a constructed repeated contribution is 0.4ⁿ for n beginning at zero. Add four terms to get 1+0.4+0.16+0.064=1.624. The exact remainder is 0.4⁴/0.6=0.042667. For a tighter tolerance of 0.001, compare N=7 and N=8: their tail bounds straddle the target. Keep terms through N=8, meaning nine contributions. Unlike a measurement uncertainty estimate, this tail comes entirely from the specified geometric mathematical model. Unmodeled changes in the ratio would require a separate argument.

lessons.title: Alternating series and error certificates
lessons.worked_example: Evaluate the four-term logarithm approximation at x=0.5 using exact fractions before rounding. Its value is 77/192, or 0.401042. Add the first omitted term 1/160 to obtain the upper enclosing partial sum. Since the signs start positive and four terms end negative, the omitted fifth term is positive, so the approximation is below ln 1.5. The interval width is 0.00625, and the actual error is 0.004423. This reasoning supplies a sign, a magnitude guarantee and an explicit partial-sum convention; reporting only “approximately 0.4” would omit all three.

lessons.title: Power series, radius and endpoints
lessons.worked_example: Analyze Σ_(n=1)∞(x−2)ⁿ/(n3ⁿ). The ratio calculation gives a radius of 3. Substitute x=−1 to obtain an alternating harmonic series and x=5 to obtain a positive harmonic series. The resulting interval is [−1,5). Evaluate x=2.5 using the dimensionless argument z=1/6 and the identity −ln(1−z), giving 0.182322. These are three separate tasks: finding the radius, classifying endpoints and computing an interior value. A single ratio inequality solves only the first task.

lessons.title: Taylor polynomials and integrated error
lessons.worked_example: Approximate the accumulation ∫₀^0.4 e^(−x)dx by integrating the cubic polynomial. The result is 0.3296. Establish the pointwise error x⁴/24 using alternating terms decreasing throughout [0,0.4], then integrate that bound to get 8.5333 × 10⁻⁵. Compare the exact value 0.329680 only after constructing the certificate. The actual error falls below the guarantee. This sequence separates an approximation, a theorem-based error statement and a reference check; knowing the reference value was not necessary for the bound.

modules.title: Geometry, parametric curves and radial amounts

lessons.title: Geometry, parametric curves and radial amounts
lessons.worked_example:
Use synthetic R=2 cm and c₀=6 arbitrary amount units per cm². Then Q=∫₀²6(1−r²/4)2πr dr. Integrate 12π(r−r³/4) to obtain 12π[r²/2−r⁴/16]₀²=12π, about 37.699112 amount units. The disk area is 4π cm², giving average density 3 amount units per cm². The center-density shortcut gives 24π amount units and doubles the correct total. An unweighted radial average would answer a different question because each radius would receive equal weight despite occupying unequal area.

The same calculation can be checked by changing variable s=r²/R². Then 2r dr=R² ds, and Q=πc₀R²∫₀¹(1−s)ds. This gives the same half factor and reveals why normalizing the radius simplifies the shape dependence. It also verifies the annular Jacobian without repeating the original polynomial integration.

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: force integration, geometric tails and sensor offset
lessons.worked_example: The synthetic corrected force readings support trapezoidal and Simpson work calculations. A four-term geometric force expansion underestimates the exact model work by about 0.261 J, within an integrated tail bound of about 0.284 J. A known constant sensor offset contributes separately to work and is removed before numerical integration.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.
Corrected the geometric-series tail arithmetic; the original approximation and exact sum are preserved.

Added an original lesson on integrals as accumulation (exact totals, trapezoidal and Simpson's rules with an error bound, improper integrals) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on Taylor approximations with Lagrange error bounds and when linearizations are accurate enough with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none, and neither do the 4 prototype-unit assessments, whose objectives are not yet linked to an outcome. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus was regenerated from the manifest: it states the current version, lists every lesson with its item and card counts, and describes the current practice and limitations (it still described only the four original units). The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described one formative check per lesson and the original numerical rules. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Fixed number formatting that an earlier authoring step left in learner-visible text: raw exponent notation (a number written with the letter e and a power of ten) and floating-point artifacts (a decimal with a long run of trailing digits) in item calculus-2-6:p2-value. No answer key, tolerance or objective changed. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added seven original lessons covering integration structure, improper-integral limits, positive and alternating series, power-series domains, Taylor and integrated error, and geometric/radial integrals; one synthetic force-work lab and a proposed 14-week schedule. Developed with Codex assistance, using existing scope references only. Still partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: Four compact prototype units remain alongside ten original readings including one synthetic-data lab; this is not equivalent to a full university semester.
The proposed 14-week sequence is unmeasured and unreviewed. Graded homework, exams, a laboratory sequence and a cumulative project are absent.
Formative item and objective links are provisional and do not establish comprehensive coverage or mastery.
All examples and observations are synthetic. Mathematical force and radial concentration models establish no device behavior, experimental protocol or biological mechanism.
New numeric prompts state their output scale and request a bare number; existing unit-entry requirements are retained. Significant figures and dimensions are not automatically assessed.
CSV and structured choices check selected calculations and distinctions; written derivations and model identification are not automatically graded.
Convergence and error bounds require their stated domains, smoothness, sign and monotonicity assumptions.
Qualified human mathematical review, accessibility review and workload measurement remain outstanding.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments, measured workload, a laboratory sequence, a cumulative graded project and named qualified review remain outstanding.
